title: Should we still teach handwriting?

turns.speaker: Bram
turns.text: Cursive is coming off the curriculum. Printing stays, joined-up writing goes.

turns.speaker: Naomi
turns.text: Which will upset a generation who were made to practise loops for years.

turns.speaker: Fern
turns.text: The defence people reach for is the note-taking research. Students writing by hand recall more than students typing.

turns.speaker: Bram
turns.text: That one's been complicated lately, hasn't it.

turns.speaker: Fern
turns.text: Considerably. The original effect was small and some replications didn't find it, and the mechanism was never really about the hand.

turns.speaker: Naomi
turns.text: It was about speed. You can't type-and-transcribe if you're slower, so you're forced to summarise.

turns.speaker: Fern
turns.text: Which means a typist told to summarise gets most of the same benefit.

turns.speaker: Bram
turns.text: So the argument is for a note-taking lesson rather than for cursive.

turns.speaker: Naomi
turns.text: The motor skill argument is separate and stronger for young children. Forming letters by hand does help letter recognition.

turns.speaker: Fern
turns.text: That's printing, though, and nobody's proposing to drop that.

turns.speaker: Bram
turns.text: What is cursive actually for now? Honest question. I sign things and that's it.

turns.speaker: Naomi
turns.text: Speed, historically. It was faster than lifting the pen, in a world where writing by hand was the only option.

turns.speaker: Fern
turns.text: Which is a solved problem that we kept teaching the solution to for fifty years.

points: Cursive is being removed from the curriculum while printing is retained.
The note-taking research, showing handwriting aids recall, has weakened under replication and had small effects.
Naomi explains the mechanism was writing speed forcing summarisation rather than handwriting itself.
Fern concludes typists instructed to summarise gain most of the same benefit, so the case supports teaching note-taking.
The motor skill argument for young children supports printing, which is not being removed.
They conclude cursive existed for speed in a handwriting-only world, a problem since solved.
